title: Cracking the PJPT: My Journey to Becoming a Certified Junior Penetration Tester
excerpt: A few months ago (January 30 2024), I successfully passed the Practical Junior Penetration Tester (PJPT) certification, offered by TCM Security. This certification stands out for its hands-on appro...
body:
Introduction

A few months ago (January 30 2024), I successfully passed the Practical Junior Penetration Tester (PJPT) certification, offered by TCM Security. This certification stands out for its hands-on approach, providing a practical penetration testing experience. Unlike other certifications in the same category, the PJPT emphasizes real-world skills, making it an excellent choice for those seeking to enhance their practical knowledge. The exam focuses primarily on Active Directory, giving you a strong foundation in a crucial area of cybersecurity. Recently, I also earned the PNPT certification, which I’ll cover in another blog. But for now, let’s dive into my experience with the PJPT.

The PJPT Course: A Comprehensive Learning Journey

When you purchase the PJPT exam voucher, it comes with access to the Practical Ethical Hacking (PEH) course at no additional cost. This course, taught by Heath Adams, the CEO and founder of TCM Security, is one of the best resources for beginners starting their ethical hacking journey. The PEH course covers a wide range of topics, from Python and Bash programming to wireless penetration testing, web exploitation, and Active Directory.

One of the key strengths of the course is that it helps you build a solid methodology for tackling real-world scenarios, which is essential for the PJPT certification. Everything you’ll encounter in the exam is covered in the course, so it’s crucial to go through the material thoroughly before attempting the exam. The comprehensive nature of the PEH course ensures that you are well-prepared, not just for the PJPT exam but for practical penetration testing challenges in general.

How to Pass: Tips from Me

First and foremost, everything comes down to one crucial skill: enumeration. How well you enumerate will determine how well you understand your target. When you know which subnet the target is in, use tools like Nmap to scan and identify open ports. Enumeration is the key, as emphasized in the course, and it’s the foundation of a successful penetration test.

Here are some tips to help you succeed:

Master Active Directory (AD): The PJPT exam heavily focuses on Active Directory, so practice this part thoroughly. Build your own AD lab as demonstrated in the course, and perform various attacks to get familiar with the exploits, their usage, and scenarios. This hands-on practice is invaluable for understanding how AD environments work in real-world situations.

Leverage Enumeration: Proper enumeration is key to understanding the AD environment and identifying potential attack paths. Visualizing the relationships within the environment can greatly assist in planning your attack strategy. Whether you prefer graphical or data-driven approaches, ensure that you fully map out and understand the environment to identify the best attack vectors.

Effective User Enumeration: Focus on thoroughly enumerating users and their access levels, which is crucial for identifying vulnerabilities. Utilizing versatile techniques for user enumeration can also aid in performing additional actions like brute-force attacks. These methods will not only help you in the PJPT exam but also prove valuable in real-world penetration tests.

Take Notes: As you practice, make sure to take detailed notes. This is a crucial part of your preparation, as it helps reinforce what you’ve learned and will be incredibly helpful during the exam. Having quick access to your notes can save you a lot of time and help you stay organized under pressure.

Practice, Practice, Practice: The most important advice I can give is to practice everything covered in the course, especially the AD section. Building your own lab, as shown in the videos, allows you to gain real experience and confidence. Play around with the setup, experiment with different attacks, and get comfortable with the tools and techniques.

And Lastly: Where to Practice?

Many people ask me what they should do to practice or if there are other resources available for practice. My answer is simple: don’t waste your time searching elsewhere. You already have everything you need with your own AD lab and the PEH course. The lab you build, as guided by the course, is the perfect environment to practice and hone your skills.

You don’t need anything beyond the PEH course. Focus your efforts on practicing within your AD lab, exploring every attack vector, and getting comfortable with the tools and techniques taught by Heath . Trust me, this is all you need to successfully pass the PJPT and build a strong foundation in penetration testing.

title: PNPT Review
excerpt: On August 1st, 2024, I proudly cleared the Practical Network Penetration Tester (PNPT) certification from TCM Security, a milestone in my cybersecurity journey. Unlike many other certifications, th...
body:
Introduction

On August 1st, 2024, I proudly cleared the Practical Network Penetration Tester (PNPT) certification from TCM Security, a milestone in my cybersecurity journey. Unlike many other certifications, the PNPT stands out for its unique, hands-on approach, offering a real-world penetration testing experience. What sets this exam apart is the lack of traditional “flags to capture.” Instead, it immerses you in practical scenarios that mirror the complexities of a live engagement, requiring you to assess, exploit, and report on vulnerabilities just like a professional pentester.

PNPT’s Essential Training

When you purchase the PNPT exam voucher, you gain access to five incredibly valuable courses: Practical Ethical Hacking (PEH), OSINT Fundamentals, External Pentest Playbook, Linux Privilege Escalation, and Windows Privilege Escalation. Each course is meticulously structured to guide you through essential penetration testing skills, with PEH standing out as the crown jewel.

As I’ve mentioned in a previous blog, PEH is exceptional, especially when compared to its competitors. It provides thorough, practical lessons that prepare you for the challenges you’ll face during the exam. From networking basics to exploitation techniques, everything tested in the exam is covered in these courses, with PEH being the cornerstone.

Moreover, the OSINT Fundamentals course is invaluable for building a solid methodology. It equips you with the skills needed for the reconnaissance phase, helping you approach your targets with precision and purpose.

How to Pass: Tips from Me

Enumeration is Key

The most critical skill you’ll need to pass the PNPT is enumeration, and that includes OSINT (Open Source Intelligence). If you don’t know your target, you won’t be able to exploit it — plain and simple. Spend time honing your OSINT and use the External Pentest Playbook (EPP) to develop a solid methodology. Understanding your target inside and out is the foundation for a successful pentest.

Master Active Directory

If you’ve taken the PJPT certification, you already know how crucial Active Directory (AD) exploitation is. The same applies here. To really master AD, you must practice, practice, and then practice some more. Set up a virtual lab and work on Active Directory attacks, as covered in the PEH course. Don’t assume you can wing it — real success comes from hands-on experience.

Take Detailed Notes

While practicing, make sure to keep thorough notes. This is vital for reinforcing what you’ve learned and will be a lifesaver during the exam. Having quick access to your notes can help you stay organized, save time, and reduce stress under pressure. Good note-taking will also help cement the techniques and methodologies you’ll use.

And Lastly: Where to Practice?

One of the most common questions I get is, “Where should I practice?” My answer is simple: don’t waste time looking elsewhere. If you’re preparing for the PNPT, everything you need is already provided within the PEH course and your own Active Directory lab. The course itself guides you in setting up a lab that perfectly mirrors real-world scenarios, making it an ideal environment to sharpen your skills.

You don’t need to seek out external resources if you’re studying with TCM Security. Their courses are comprehensive, covering all the attack vectors and tools you’ll need to know. Focus your energy on mastering the techniques taught by Heath Adams in the PEH course, and practice extensively in your lab. That’s all you need to successfully pass the PNPT and build a solid foundation for your penetration testing career.

title: I Took the PMRP. Here’s What Actually Mattered.
excerpt: The premise is simple. You’re the new hire on a malware research team, and on day one somebody drops a pile of unknown samples on your desk and says “figure these out, clients need reports.” You ge...
body:
The setup

The premise is simple. You’re the new hire on a malware research team, and on day one somebody drops a pile of unknown samples on your desk and says “figure these out, clients need reports.” You get Windows and Linux analysis boxes, roughly five days to do the analysis, and two more days to write it all up.

I had seven samples. A couple went down fast. A couple of others had me staring at the screen for hours before anything made sense.

How it’s scored

Samples come in three tiers: easy, medium, hard. The hard ones are worth the most, which is fair, because that’s where you find out whether you understand the malware or just recognize what it looks like. There’s also a detection part where you write YARA rules for whatever samples you attempted. Passing is around 72%.

The catch is that the report is a separate hard requirement. You can rack up points and still fail if the report isn’t up to standard. Once I understood that, the whole exam made more sense. Reversing skill matters, sure, but the report is where your analysis either holds up or quietly falls apart.

Easy, medium, hard

The easy samples respond well to the usual routine: strings, imports, detonate it somewhere safe, watch what changes. But don’t go in thinking they’re free points. A few had small details that made the difference between a lazy note and a useful one, and I went back to some of them more than once to double check myself.

Medium is where the exam starts pushing back. One observation isn’t enough anymore. You have to connect what you saw statically with what happens at runtime, and you have to keep asking yourself: did the sample do that, or did my environment do that? I didn’t expect that question to matter as much as it did. It turned out to be one of the most important habits of the whole week.

The hard samples were mostly a test of patience. A lot of debugger time, a lot of notepad time. Go through one function, write down what I thought it did, run it again, see if I was right. Sometimes I wasn’t. The only reason I caught those mistakes is that I’d written down why I believed them in the first place.

So if you’re thinking about it: get really solid on the fundamentals first. A sample looking simple doesn’t mean it is.

Time (you have less than you think)

Five days sounds like a lot. It isn’t. One sample can easily eat an entire afternoon, and early on I let that happen way too often because I wanted to understand every single detail before moving on. Bad trade. What works better is getting a rough picture of every sample first, then going back for depth where the points justify it.

The other thing that saved me: writing notes while I worked, not after. By the time report days came around, most of the report already existed in my notes, just messier.

The report is the actual exam

If you only remember one thing from this post, make it this one. Treat the report as the main deliverable, not something you scramble through at the end.

It needs an executive summary, a sample summary table with the required fields, and a proper walkthrough per sample: basic info, static analysis, dynamic analysis, IOCs. The bar is basically “could a client read this and do something with it?” Explain what it does, how it does it, how you know, and what to look for to detect it. A wall of hashes and strings with no explanation won’t get you much, no matter how clever the work behind it was.

I also came to appreciate being upfront about limits. Some behaviour in a lab only happens because of what your environment is simulating. Some things only showed up after I’d tweaked the sample or the setup. Good reports make that split obvious: here’s what the original, untouched sample did, and here’s what I only saw after modifying something. That’s what makes a report trustworthy, and honestly it’s what the examiners are looking for.

What I’d do differently

Less chasing the perfect answer on each sample, more making sure the report told one coherent story across all of them. And I’d write YARA rules as I went, while the strings and behaviours were still fresh in my head, instead of leaving them all to the end. Future me was not thrilled with past me on that one.

Overall

It’s a good test of whether you can work as an actual malware analyst or a learner like me. It’s not a trivia quiz. It rewards people who slow down enough to get things right and then explain them clearly.

If you’re going for it, plan to write about as much as you analyze. For me, that ended up being the part that counted most.

Originally published on Medium: https://shinchansecureshell.medium.com/what-the-pmrp-exam-taught-me-about-malware-analysis-8182025aaed4
